modules.comments:
d3-force's forces in PureScript, with no JavaScript for the algorithms,
and what the Rust kernel has that d3 does not.

Each force has its own module with an `initialize` and an `apply`; this
module gathers them into one `Force` type and gives d3's loop: cool,
apply each force, move the nodes, and then (the Rust kernel's addition)
apply any hard constraint and put pinned nodes back.

The d3 forces are held to d3-force 3.0.0 bit for bit, and the others to
the Rust kernel built at 64 bits, by `test/differential.mjs`.

`tick`, `applyForces` and the order of a tick are ported from d3-force
3.0.0, `simulation.js` (ISC, Copyright 2010-2021 Mike Bostock); see
LICENSE.

modules.comments:
Group cohesion: pull each node toward the centroid of its group.

Not in d3. The rule is the Rust kernel's (`apply_cohesion` in
`force-kernel/src/forces.rs`), and the two are held to each other bit
for bit by `test/differential.mjs`.

The centroid of a group is the mean position of its members whose
position is finite, summed in node order. For every node in a group
whose position is finite:

```
v += (centroid - position) * strength * alpha
```

A node in no group is left alone and counts toward no centroid. A
strength of `NaN` counts as zero, and such a node still counts toward
its group's centroid.

declarations.comments:
`group` and `strength` are asked once per node when the force is
initialized.
declarations.title: Config

declarations.comments: An initialized cohesion force: the members of each group, in node order.
declarations.title: Cohesion

declarations.comments:
The force only changes velocities, so each group's centroid can be
taken just before its members are pulled.
declarations.title: apply

modules.name: Hylograph.Forces.Cohesion

modules.comments:
The collision force: treat each node as a circle and push overlapping
circles apart.

Ported from d3-force 3.0.0, `collide.js` (ISC, Copyright 2010-2021 Mike
Bostock); see LICENSE.

The shape is the many-body force's. Each iteration builds a quadtree of
where the nodes are about to be (`x + vx`), turns it into a chain of
`Region`s that each know the largest radius inside them (d3's `prepare`),
and walks the chain once per node. A walk is pure: it returns the node's
new velocity and the new velocities of the nodes it pushed, and those
are written when the walk has returned. That is the same as d3 writing
them as it goes, because a walk meets each other node at most once and
never reads back a velocity it has changed.

Like d3, this looks only at the newest of several nodes at exactly the
same place; the older ones are not collided with until something else
moves them.

declarations.comments:
d3's `forceCollide` settings. `radius` is asked once per node when the
force is initialized.
declarations.title: Config

declarations.comments:
d3's defaults: radius 1, full strength, one iteration; and the two
things d3 does not have turned off.

Those two are the Rust kernel's "yielding collision" (`apply_collide`
in `force-kernel/src/forces.rs`), held to it by `test/differential.mjs`:

- `alphaScaled`: the strength used is `strength * alpha`, so the
  collision weakens as the simulation cools and gives way to forces
  that hold a node at a place;
- `include`: a pair is tested only if both of its nodes are included. A
  node left out neither pushes nor is pushed. (It is still in the
  quadtree, where it can only widen the search.)
declarations.title: defaultConfig

modules.comments:
Containment: keep each node inside a region. A soft force steers a node
back in before the nodes move; an optional hard confine puts it back in
after they have.

Not in d3. The rules are the Rust kernel's (`Region::project`,
`apply_contain` and `constrain` in `force-kernel/src/forces.rs`), and the
two are held to each other bit for bit by `test/differential.mjs`.

**The body.** A node is kept inside as a rectangle of half-width `w` and
half-height `h`, grown all round by a radius `r`: a circle when `w` and
`h` are zero, a plain rectangle when `r` is, a rounded rectangle
otherwise.

**Projection.** `project region r w h x y` is where such a body centred
on (x, y) has to move its centre to, to lie inside the region. A centre
already far enough inside comes back unchanged.

- Rectangle: clamp x to `[x0 + (r + w), x1 - (r + w)]` and y to
  `[y0 + (r + h), y1 - (r + h)]`. If the rectangle is narrower than the
  body on an axis, that coordinate goes to the middle of the rectangle.
- Circle: the body counts as the circle round it, of radius
  `r + sqrt(w*w + h*h)` (exact for a round body, a little cautious for a
  rectangle). With `R' = max(R - r - sqrt(w*w + h*h), 0)`, a centre
  further than `R'` from the region's centre `c` moves to
  `c + (p - c) * (R' / |p - c|)`.
- Convex polygon: one pass visits the edges in order; for each, with
  inward unit normal `n` and `d` the signed distance from the centre (as
  it now is) to the edge's line, positive inside, the body reaches
  `s = (r + |n.x| * w) + |n.y| * h` towards the edge, and a centre with
  `d < s` moves along the normal by `s - d`. Passes repeat until one
  moves nothing, eight at most.

**Soft.** For every node with a region, with `a = position + velocity`
finite and `c = project region r w h a`: `v += (c - a) * strength`. Not
scaled by alpha: it is a constraint, like collide.

**Hard.** After the nodes have moved, every node with a region and a
finite position is put at `project region r w h position`, and its
velocity changes by the same amount, so that the velocity is still the
step the node actually took. Pinned coordinates are then put back: a
pin beats a region.

modules.comments:
The directional link constraint: keep each link's target at least a gap
beyond its source along an axis (children below their parents).

Not in d3. The rule is the Rust kernel's (`apply_directional` in
`force-kernel/src/forces.rs`), and the two are held to each other bit
for bit by `test/differential.mjs`.

With `u` the unit axis, and working on anticipated positions
`a = position + velocity`, for each iteration and each link in order,
reading the velocities as the links before it left them:

```
d = (a_target - a_source) . u
if d < gap:
  push = (gap - d) * strength * alpha
  v_target += u * push * bias
  v_source -= u * push * (1 - bias)
```

where `bias` is d3's link bias, so the better connected end moves less.
A link already satisfied is not touched: the force pushes apart and
never pulls. A link whose gap or strength is `NaN` is left alone.

That is a force, scaled by alpha and shared with everything else that
pushes, so the gap it leaves can be well short of the one asked for.

HARD. With `hard: true` the gap asked for is the gap kept: after the
nodes have moved, with the hard containments and in the order the
forces are listed, the links are projected. A node is HELD along the
axis if it is pinned on a coordinate the axis has a part in (`fx` when
`u.x` is not 0, `fy` when `u.y` is not 0; here, whatever the config's
`heldX` and `heldY` say). One pass takes each link in order, on the
positions as the links before it left them, both ends finite:

```
d = (p_target - p_source) . u
if d < gap:
  short = gap - d
  if the target is not held:      p_target += u * short,  v_target += u * short
  else if the source is not held: p_source -= u * short,  v_source -= u * short
  else:                           nothing
```

So the target gives way, and the source only where the target cannot.
Passes repeat until one moves nothing, thirty-two at most (a chain of
links listed child-first needs one pass per link; a cycle of links can
never be satisfied and stops at the limit). The velocity changes with
the position, as a containment's clamp does, so the node does not fly
back next tick. The soft force above is applied as well, unless its
strengths are 0.

declarations.comments:
`gap` and `strength` are asked once per link when the force is
initialized. The axis need not be a unit vector: it is normalised, and
an axis of zero or infinite length becomes (0, 1), which is "below" on a
screen. `heldX` and `heldY` matter only to the hard projection, and are
asked each time it runs: `Node.pinnedX` and `Node.pinnedY` are the ones
to give for nodes with `fx` and `fy`.
declarations.title: Config

modules.comments:
The many-body force: every node attracts or repels every other, with the
far field approximated by Barnes-Hut over a quadtree.

Ported from d3-force 3.0.0, `manyBody.js` (ISC, Copyright 2010-2021 Mike
Bostock); see LICENSE. The arithmetic, its order and the draws from the
random source follow d3 line for line, so the velocities agree with
d3-force to the bit.

Each application has three steps, and the first two are pure:

1. build the quadtree of the nodes' positions (`Quadtree.build`);
2. turn it into a chain of `Cluster`s: d3's `accumulate`, which gives
   every square its total strength and centre, done together with the
   threading that lets the walk run without a stack;
3. for each node in turn, walk the chain to get the node's new velocity,
   and write it.

The chain is the tree in d3's visiting order. Each cluster knows the
cluster to go to when its square has to be opened (`inside`) and the one
to go to when the square is finished with (`after`), so "visit, and skip
the children if the callback says so" becomes a loop that follows one
pointer or the other.

declarations.comments:
d3's `forceManyBody` settings. `strength` is asked once per node when the
force is initialized; negative repels.
declarations.title: Config

declarations.comments:
d3's defaults: strength -30, theta 0.9, distances from 1 to infinity,
between every pair of nodes.
declarations.title: defaultConfig

declarations.comments:
Which pairs of nodes the force acts between. Only `EveryPair` is d3's;
the other two are the Rust kernel's scoped many-body (`apply_many_body`
in `force-kernel/src/forces.rs`), which `test/differential.mjs` holds
this to bit for bit.

- `WithinGroups`: for each group in ascending order of its number, d3's
  many-body is applied to that group's nodes alone: its own quadtree,
  its nodes in node order. A node in no group neither exerts nor feels
  anything.
- `BetweenGroups`: d3's many-body over all the nodes, followed by
  `WithinGroups` with every strength negated. With theta 0 that is the
  sum over pairs in different groups; with theta above 0 it is the
  difference of two Barnes-Hut approximations. A node in no group
  interacts with every node.

The random source is drawn from in that order too.
declarations.title: Scope

`BetweenGroups`).

kernel's (`kinetic_energy`, `max_displacement`, `max_acceleration` and

holds the two to each other bit for bit.

where the nodes were, so they are kept by a `Watch`: tell it when a tick
begins and when it ends, and ask it afterwards.

nodes, in order, of `vx * vx` and then `vy * vy`, halved. After a tick
the velocity is the step the node took in it, so this falls toward zero
as the layout settles.

modules.name: Hylograph.Forces.Measure

modules.comments:
The simulation node, as the rest of Hylograph hands it over: a JavaScript
object typed as a record, which the forces update in place.

PureScript can read a record field but has no way to assign one, and
nothing in the package set does it either (`Record.ST` left `record` at
4.0). So this module holds the package's only foreign code: four
assignments, one line each, in `Node.js`. Every piece of arithmetic is
PureScript.

The fields are mutable behind the type system's back, so the forces follow
one rule: a mutable field is read where its value is used, in the
arguments of the write that replaces it or inside a pure function that
returns before anything is written. It is never bound to a name across a
write.

modules.comments:
The part of d3-quadtree that d3-force uses: build a tree from a set of
points, once, and hand it to a force to walk.

Ported from d3-quadtree 3.0.1 (ISC, Copyright 2010-2021 Mike Bostock);
see LICENSE.

d3 inserts the points one at a time into a mutable tree. This builds the
same tree from the top down, without mutation: a square that holds no
point is `Empty`, one that holds a single location is a `Leaf`, and any
other is a `Branch` of its four quarters. That is the tree d3's insertion
arrives at whatever the order, because d3 splits a square exactly when a
second location lands in it. Two things do depend on insertion order and
are kept: the points of a leaf run newest first, as d3's `next` chain
does, and the extent starts from the unit square at the floor of the
smallest coordinates and doubles until it covers the largest.

The squares themselves are not stored. A force recomputes them as it
walks, halving from the root's extent with the same `(x0 + x1) / 2` that
d3's `visit` uses, so the bounds agree to the bit.

declarations.comments: A location and whatever the force keeps there.
declarations.title: Point

declarations.comments:
A quadtree. The quarters of a `Branch` are in d3's order: top-left,
top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right, where "right" is `x >= middle` and

modules.comments:
Rectangle collision: push overlapping axis-aligned rectangles apart
along the axis on which they overlap least.

Not in d3. The rule is the Rust kernel's (`apply_rect_collide` in
`force-kernel/src/forces.rs`), and the two are held to each other bit
for bit by `test/differential.mjs`.

Node i is a rectangle of half-width `w_i` and half-height `h_i` centred
on its anticipated position `a_i = position + velocity`. A node is HELD
on an axis if it cannot be moved along it: it is pinned there (`fx` for
x, `fy` for y; here, whatever the config's `heldX` and `heldY` say). One
iteration:

1. Take `a_i` for every node that takes part, all at once, before
   anything moves.
2. For every node i that takes part, and every other node j that takes
   part and may collide with it (see "Who collides"), both `a` finite,
   taking j in ascending order:

   ```
   dx = a_i.x - a_j.x          dy = a_i.y - a_j.y
   ox = (w_i + w_j) - |dx|     oy = (h_i + h_j) - |dy|
   ```

   The pair overlaps when `ox > 0` and `oy > 0`. If it does, the push is
   along x if `ox <= oy` and along y otherwise. If i is held on that
   axis, nothing more happens for this pair. Otherwise

   ```
   share = 1                      if j is held on that axis
         = A_j / (A_i + A_j)      otherwise, with A = w * h
                                  (1/2 if A_i + A_j is not above 0)
   push  = s * overlap * strength * share
   v_i[axis] += push
   ```

   where `s` is the sign of dx (or dy): +1 if positive, -1 if negative,
   and if exactly zero, -1 when i < j and +1 when i > j.

So a held rectangle is never moved, and what overlaps it takes the whole
correction; two free rectangles share it, the smaller moving more.

THE SQUEEZE. A wide rectangle nearly always overlaps another least
vertically, so it is only ever pushed up or down; caught between two
things that do not give way (two pinned dots, a dot and a packed row of
other labels) the pushes cancel and it sits on both for ever. With
`squeezed: goesThrough`, after the last iteration of one application of
the force, for each node i and each axis it is not held on: let `up` be
the sum of the positive pushes step 2 gave it on that axis over all the
iterations, and `down` the sum of the negative ones, as a magnitude. If
both are above 0 the node is squeezed, and it goes with one side and
ignores the other:

```
v_i[axis] += down     if it goes up     (the downward pushes are undone)
v_i[axis] -= up       if it goes down
```

It goes the way it was already moving, if it was moving: with `w` its
velocity on that axis as it was when the force was applied, if
`|w| > 0.001 * (up + down)` it goes up when `w > 0` and down when
`w < 0`. Otherwise (a velocity that small is what is left of a movement
long over, or the last of a pull dying away) it goes with the stronger
side: up if `up > down`, down if `up < down`, and if they are equal, up
when i is odd and down when it is even.

Going the way it is moving is what makes this resolve: the rectangle
keeps on through whatever was squeezing it, a dot or another rectangle,
until it is clear, where a rule that only compared the two sides would
turn round as soon as it went deeper into the weaker one. It suits
rectangles that nothing else is pressing together. Under a force that
keeps pressing (a pull to a point that a pinned body is standing on) a
squeeze is permanent and the rectangle will be walked through its
neighbour, so let such a pull die away before expecting rest. With
`squeezed: staysPut`, the default, step 2 is all there is.

Who collides. A node left out by `include` collides with nothing and
nothing collides with it. With groups, `pairs` restricts the pairs: only
two nodes of the same group (`withinGroups`), or only two nodes not of
the same group (`betweenGroups`; a node in no group is in a different
group from everyone).

Every correction in an iteration comes from the same anticipated
positions, so no node is favoured by its index. Not scaled by alpha, as
d3's collide is not.

The quadtree only finds the rectangles that overlap a given one. They
are then put in index order before their corrections are added, which
makes the result the same, bit for bit, as the loop over all pairs.

declarations.comments:
`halfWidth`, `halfHeight`, `include` and `group` are asked once per node
when the force is initialized; a half-extent of `NaN` counts as zero.
`heldX` and `heldY` say whether a node cannot be moved along an axis,
and are asked every time the force is applied, since pins come and go:
`Node.pinnedX` and `Node.pinnedY` are the ones to give for nodes with
`fx` and `fy`.
declarations.title: Config

declarations.comments:

modules.comments:
Snapshot and restore: everything that changes as a simulation runs, as
one immutable value.

The forces keep no state between ticks (each rebuilds what it needs from
the nodes), so what changes is alpha, the random source, and each node's
position, velocity and pins. Restoring a snapshot and running N ticks
gives exactly what N more ticks would have given when it was taken, as
long as the forces and settings are the same; they are configuration,
not state, and are not in the snapshot.

The Rust kernel has the same pair (`snapshot` and `restore` in
`force-kernel/src/lib.rs`), and `test/differential.mjs` checks both
against each other across a restore.

declarations.title: Snapshot

random source, and the nodes.

declarations.comments:
Put the nodes and the random source back as the snapshot recorded
them, and return the alpha to give the next tick. The nodes are matched
by place; if there are more or fewer than were recorded, the extra ones
on either side are left alone.

modules.comments:
The towards force: a spring from each node to its own target point.

Not in d3. The rule is the Rust kernel's (`apply_towards` in
`force-kernel/src/forces.rs`), and the two are held to each other bit
for bit by `test/differential.mjs`. For every node with a target whose
coordinates are both numbers:

```
vx += (targetX - x) * strength * alpha
vy += (targetY - y) * strength * alpha
```

A node whose target has a `NaN` in it is left alone, and a strength of
`NaN` counts as zero.

declarations.comments:
`target` and `strength` are asked once per node when the force is
initialized. To move the targets, initialize again.
